Miner Willy jumped. He jumped again. But then, Willy fell into a deep pit.
"Oh no!" Ben cried. "He cannot get out. The game is too hard."
Mia looked at the screen. She saw a different path.
"Wait," Mia said. "Do not go straight. Try the path to the left."
Ben moved the joystick. Willy hopped to the left. He found a hidden bridge.
"You did it!" Ben shouted.
Willy jumped over the bridge and grabbed a shiny key. 
"I like this game," Ben said. "When it is hard, we just have to try a new way."
Mia smiled. They both loved playing with Miner Willy in his cave.

A tiny line of color appeared at the top. Then a dot. Then a little corner of a picture, bit by bit. Hippo popped up in the middle of the screen. "Hello! I am Hippo. I live inside Speccy. The picture is coming slowly, but every small bit helps it grow." Tim looked closer. "A tiny dot can make a big picture?" "Yes!" said Hippo. "Each little dot is like a small star. Put them together and you get a whole sky." Ben giggled. "Small things can do big things." The picture grew and grew until a castle with tall towers filled the screen. Tim jumped up. "It is finished!" Hippo waved his small pink hoof. "See? Small bits, big castle."

Emma wanted to make music, but she did not know how. Tom had an idea. "Speccy can make beeps. Let us ask Hippo." Hippo appeared in a little window on the screen and blinked his big round eyes. "I can teach you the word BEEP," he said. "Type BEEP and a number, then ENTER." Emma typed BEEP one, comma, two. Nothing happened. "It does not work," she said, a little sad. Tom frowned and thought. "Maybe we should try a different number. Let us try a new way." Emma typed BEEP two, comma, four. Beep! A low sound came out of the TV. Emma giggled and jumped up. She typed more numbers, and soon the beeps made a happy little song. Hippo clapped his hooves. "You found a new way, and now Speccy sings!" Tom smiled. "Your music sounds great, Emma." Emma bowed to the TV, and the beeps went boop, boop, boop.

It was night, and the house was quiet. Tom was in bed, and his little brother Sam was in the room too. The Speccy was turned on, and its screen was dark and blue. "Hippo, will you tell us a story?" asked Sam. The screen glowed. Letters appeared, one at a time, in soft green. "Once upon a time," wrote Hippo, "there was a sleepy brown owl who lived in a tall tree." Sam yawned a big yawn. Tom listened to the owl and the moon and the wind. The letters came slowly, but Tom did not mind. At the end, the owl went to sleep, and so did Sam. Tom whispered, "Thank you, Hippo." The screen wrote back: "You are welcome, Tom. Good night." Tom turned off the lamp. The little Speccy glowed softly in the dark, and Tom smiled. Thank you is a nice thing to say, he thought before he fell asleep.

Lily's eyes grew wide. "It has a rainbow stripe on the corner!"
"Thank you, Grandma," said Zoe. "This is the best surprise ever."
Grandma smiled. "You are welcome, my dear. Let us plug it in and see if it still works."
They plugged in the wires and turned on the TV. The screen flickered, and the old message appeared.
"It works!" shouted Lily.
"Thank you for helping me find it," said Grandma. "I am glad to share it with you."
Lily hugged her grandma tightly. "Thank you for keeping it safe all these years!"

Ben and Anna were playing a game about Dizzy, the funny egg with red boxing gloves. Dizzy had to find things and help his friends in a big, colorful castle.

Dizzy rolled across the floor and pushed the heavy stone away. The mouse scurried out, squeaking happily.
Hippo, the little magenta hippo who lives inside Speccy, clapped his feet on the screen. "Well done, Dizzy! Helping friends is the best thing to do."
Anna smiled. "Thank you, Hippo, for cheering us on."
"Thank you for helping Dizzy," said Hippo with a bright grin. "You are very kind to the little mouse."
Ben nodded. "Dizzy would never leave a friend behind."
The mouse ran off to find its family, and Dizzy went on his way across the castle.
"Thank you for playing with me," said Anna, giving the Speccy a gentle pat.
"Thank you for being such good friends," said Hippo.

Hippo was slow, so he thought for a long time. Then, one letter at a time, a story came onto the screen. It was about a brave little duck who crossed a big blue pond to find her mother.
Kim clapped her hands. "I love it! Can you tell another one?"
"Yes, but first let me tell you something," said Hippo. "Speccy forgets everything when it is turned off. If you want to keep my stories, you must save them on a tape."
Sue typed SAVE and pressed ENTER. The tape player sang its loud, screechy song while the story was saved. Kim watched the stripes dance on the edge of the screen.
"Now we can hear it again tomorrow," said Kim happily. Sue held the cassette up to the light and smiled.
Hippo's ears wiggled. "Not that smart, but it works!" he said proudly, and both girls giggled.
<|endoftext|>
Tom and Jack were building a tower of game boxes next to Speccy. The desk was crowded with papers, and the little black computer was squashed against the wall. Suddenly a puff of warm air came out of its side.
"Oh no, it is getting too hot," said Jack. "It needs space to breathe."
Tom looked around the messy room. "We must move all these papers. Then Speccy can have some air."
Jack wanted to hurry, so he pushed too fast. A pile of tapes slid off the desk and fell onto the floor with a clatter. Tom laughed, and Jack laughed too.
"Let us pick them up together," said Tom. They gathered every tape, one by one, and made a neat stack on the shelf.
Then they carried Speccy into the open space in the middle of the room, away from the wall and the papers. Soon the warm feeling went away, and the little rainbow stripe on its corner looked cool and bright again.
"We helped Speccy," said Tom proudly.
"Yes, and we helped each other too," said Jack, giving Tom a big high five.

It was a rainy day, and the whole family stayed at home. Lily and her little brother Leo wanted to play with Speccy. Mom turned on the old TV, and the white screen said hello.
Hippo popped up and waved his small pink hand. "Hello, Lily! Hello, Leo! Do you want to make a game together?"
"Yes!" said Leo, jumping up and down.
Lily typed a short program with the soft rubber keys. She wanted a little dog to jump across the screen. Her fingers went squish, squish, squish.
But when she pressed RUN, Speccy said: "Nonsense in BASIC." Lily frowned. "The dog will not jump! What did I do wrong?"
Hippo thought hard. "Look at the third line. You wrote a word that Speccy does not know. Fix it and try again."
Lily fixed the mistake and pressed RUN. The dog jumped high, and then it jumped again. Leo clapped his hands, and Dad and Mom came in to watch.
"Mistakes are okay," said Mom with a smile. "Fix them and keep going, and you will learn something new."

"I want to make the spaceman jump now!" said Amy. "No, I want to shoot!" said Rosa.
Their game on Speccy was about a tiny robot. The robot was very small, but it had to fix a big broken bridge with its little hands.
Amy looked at the robot for a long time. "Look, it does not need to be big. It just needs to keep trying, one step at a time."
Rosa smiled. "Small things can do big things," she said. "Let us take turns."
They took turns, and each one pushed the robot forward a tiny bit. Slowly, the bridge grew longer, one brick at a time.
At last, the robot reached the far side, and the screen flashed bright yellow.
"We did it!" Amy and Rosa said together, and they both laughed and hugged.

Anna and Tom had a special Speccy with one hundred twenty-eight K of memory. Anna's dad said it could play music with three voices at once.
"Let us make a song!" said Tom. He typed some BEEP lines, one by one, and pressed ENTER. The first try made a noise like a sad goose.
"Oh no," Tom groaned. "This sounds terrible. I want to stop."
Hippo's small face popped up in the corner of the screen. "Do not give up," he said. "Every musician makes mistakes. Change one thing and listen again."
Anna changed one line. Speccy played a smooth little tune, and then a second voice came in, bright and happy. Then a third voice joined, and the whole room was full of music.
Tom jumped out of his chair and danced around. "We made a song with three voices!" he shouted.
"Not that smart, but it works," said Hippo, wiggling with joy.

Sue and Tim were playing a racing game on Speccy when the little black box began to feel hot. A thin smell drifted up from the side, and Tim frowned. "Something is wrong," he said.
Sue touched the top, and it was warm. They had put Speccy inside a soft cushioned box with no air holes at all.
"Oops, we covered it up," said Tim. "Speccy needs space to breathe. That was my mistake, because I put the box on top of it."
"We can fix it," said Sue. They lifted the lid, took Speccy out, and set it on the table near the open window.
"Next time, we should check the air before we play," Sue said. "Mistakes happen, but the trick is to fix them quickly."
Soon the warm feeling went away, and the race car on the screen zoomed around the track again. Tim laughed with relief.
Hippo popped up in the corner of the screen and waved his pink hand. "Good job, friends! Fixing a mistake is very brave. Not that smart, but it works!"
Speccy beeped a happy little beep, and the race went on.

Sam drew a bright red ball on his Speccy. He was very proud of it. The ball was round and shiny, and it sat in the middle of a green field.
Lily came to look. "Why is the edge of your ball flickering?" she asked. "It looks like it is shaking."
Sam leaned closer. The red ball sat right on a square that also had green grass, and the colors were jumping into each other.
"That is color clash," said Sam, sighing. "Speccy can show only two colors in each little square of eight by eight dots. The colors spill onto their neighbors."
"That is so strange," said Lily. "But your ball is still nice!"
Sam felt sad anyway. He wanted it to be perfect. "Maybe I should give up," he said.
"Do not give up," said Lily. "Move the ball a tiny bit to the left, so it sits on its own square."
Sam moved the ball. The red edge became sharp and clean, and the grass stayed green.
Hippo's voice came softly from the screen. "Color clash is a tricky puzzle, Sam. But you are clever, and you solved it!"

"It is so small," said Rosa. "How can such a little box do so much?"
Hippo popped up on the screen with a big grin. "Small things can do big things," he said. "Look what I can draw."
He drew a big yellow sun, a green tree, and a blue river with fish swimming in it.
Emma clapped her hands. "That is beautiful, Hippo!"
Rosa laughed. "I did not know a little computer could make so much. Speccy is a wonderful friend."
Rosa wrote her own name with the rubber keys, very slowly, letter by letter.
Speccy beeped happily, as if it liked its new friends very much.

Tim and Ben wanted to load a game from a tape. The tape player was small, but when the tape started, it sang a loud screechy song.
"Such a small machine, and such a loud song," said Ben with a laugh.
Tim giggled. "Small things can do big things! Look at the screen."
The stripes on the screen flashed red, light blue, blue and yellow. Slowly, the picture of a race car came in bit by bit.
They did not give up, and they waited patiently for each piece to appear. The race car gleamed in the sunshine on the screen.
Then they played the game all afternoon, taking turns on the joystick. The little tape player was the hero of the day.
The little Speccy seemed to be listening too, and it beeped softly now and then.
"Thank you, tape player," said Tim, patting the machine gently.

Leo made a tiny game on Speccy. In it, a cat chased a mouse around the screen, and the mouse was very quick.
But every time Leo made the cat move, it fell off the edge of the screen and disappeared.
"This is so hard," said Leo, and he rubbed his eyes. "The cat keeps falling."
Kim leaned over his shoulder and looked at the lines of the program. "Do not give up," she said. "Try moving the cat more slowly."
Leo changed one line of the program, and then he pressed RUN. The cat walked carefully along the floor and stopped at the edge.
Then it ran after the mouse. The mouse hid behind a small box, and the cat sat down and waited for it to come out.
Leo cheered and jumped up from his chair. "I did not give up! The cat caught the mouse!"
Kim laughed. "You were patient and clever, Leo. Speccy is proud of you too."

The edge of the screen flashed red and light blue stripes. Then blue and yellow stripes came, and they danced very fast.
"What is happening?" asked Timmy.
"The computer is loading the game," said Ben. "The picture comes one bit at a time."
Slowly, a tiny corner of a castle appeared on the screen. Then a flag. Then a little window and a bridge.
"It is like building a puzzle," said Timmy. "Every piece comes out one at a time."
"That is why we have to be patient," Ben said. "Learning is fun when we watch carefully."
At last, the whole castle stood on the screen. Timmy shouted, "We did it! The castle is ready!"

Amy sighed. "Small things can take a long time."

Slowly, the words came onto the screen. A brave mouse, a tiny boat and a sea full of stars.
Amy smiled. The story was worth every minute of waiting. "Thank you, Hippo. You are slow, but your stories are wonderful."
Hippo blushed pink and wiggled his ears. "Thank you for waiting for me!"

"Then what can we do?" asked Emma.
"Maybe we just need some space between them," said Mia. "Small things can do big things, if we place them with care."
They moved the butterfly a little way from the flower. The fuzzy edges disappeared.
Emma clapped her hands. "Now the butterfly can fly freely!"
Mia smiled. "And the flower can stay where it is, bright and red."
Together, they made a whole garden of clean squares. It was the most beautiful picture they had ever made on a Speccy.

The last level of Manic Miner was the hardest of all. Bob and Anna had been stuck on it for a whole week.
"I think we should give up," sighed Bob.
"Do not give up," said Anna. "We have come so far. Willy needs us."
They pressed the joystick and watched Willy jump. He landed on the wrong ledge and fell into the spider's hole on Speccy.
Bob groaned and threw his hands up. "This game is too hard!"
Anna took the joystick. "Let me try. We will take it slowly, one jump at a time."
Hippo, the little hippo who lived inside Speccy, cheered from the corner. "Keep going, friends! Hard levels make the best victories."
Anna jumped Willy over the spider, onto the moving platform, and up to the shiny key. The key sparkled, and the door opened with a clang.
"We did it!" shouted Bob.
Anna grinned. "I told you. Do not give up, Bob."
